A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same neuron-centric model-fusion work, despite retitling. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original VGG and ViT fusion experiments, a MNIST clustering analysis, and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

after.justification: v2 reports original fusion experiments, additional medical and ImageNet evaluations, compression results, and robustness studies in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

M1.justification: The grouping-and-fitting framework remains intact. v2 adds HF-Gradient, combining Hungarian matching with gradient-based fitting, whereas v1 considered only KF for the nonlinear gradient variant (v1 Section 4.3.2; v2 Section 4.2.2).

E1.justification: v2 adds BloodMNIST blood-cell classification, Tiny-ImageNet fusion, ImageNet-1k task fusion, and teacher-to-student ResNet compression on CIFAR-100. The MNIST clustering example is replaced by a CIFAR-10 example. These substantially expand the represented domains and evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates activation- and weight-based Transformer OTFusion in the ViT comparisons, previously absent because v1 could not adapt its implementation. ZipIt! enters the sharded VGG and ImageNet comparisons. Whole-model KD receives explicit comparison rows alongside the head-only comparator, described as last-layer KD in v1 and LP in v2.

E3.justification: CIFAR-100 ViTs change from patch size 8 and MLP width 384 to patch size 4 and MLP width 1536. ViT fusion budgets change from 7000 sharded/6000 full-dataset samples to 5000. Gradient configurations switch to AdamW with head weighting disabled, and fine-tuning settings change. Added experiments introduce compression and augmentation protocols; activation-based Transformer OTFusion uses 200 samples versus 5000 for the proposed methods.

E4.justification: v2 adds fusion-data-size and augmentation ablations, unequal-width fusion tests, compression-versus-KD comparisons, and an end-to-end runtime analysis. The three-MLP MNIST clustering illustration becomes a two-VGG CIFAR-10 analysis including DeepLIFT and adjusted Rand indices (Figure 3). These substantially broaden tests of sensitivity, mechanisms and applicability.

E5.justification: Four-way full-dataset ViT results change from three seeds with standard deviations in v1 to a single seed without dispersion in v2 Table 18. v2 also reports variability for its new end-to-end timing measurements. Most retained accuracy comparisons continue using means and standard deviations.

E6.justification: Many results are replaced or added. Two-way full-dataset CIFAR-100 KF-Gradient with uniform scores reports 72.7% zero-shot/73.9% fine-tuned in v1 Table 14 versus 63.0%/75.2% in v2 Table 18; changed settings prevent interpreting this as a controlled performance comparison. New benchmarks and analyses add substantial results, while v1's non-IID CIFAR-100 ViT tables and Conductance runtime entries disappear.

T1.justification: Theorem 2 now explicitly fixes all preceding levels and limits its guarantees to the current level. A new NP-hardness discussion explains the exclusion of joint optimization across levels. The decomposition, principal proofs and 9-plus-epsilon approximation bound otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: v2 adds flexible open-source baseline reimplementation as an explicit contribution and qualifies architectural generality as applicability to networks modularizable into a DAG of levels. The central representation-matching and neuron-saliency contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the applicability and cost interpretation: it distinguishes one-shot fusion from iterative federated learning, recommends local attribution estimation under skew, and argues that slower fusion can be offset by avoided fine-tuning. Data augmentation becomes an explicit mitigation for data dependence. v1's interpretation of its two distinct gradient-optimization regimes is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices E–F add linear regularization strengths, attribution-data and score-selection instructions, ResNet implementation provenance, and dataset-specific architecture and fine-tuning details. Fusion configurations are substantially revised. Conversely, v1's explicit base-training epoch schedule is replaced by training until convergence, reducing reproducibility detail in that respect.

R1.justification: The introduction adds positioning around linear mode connectivity, divergent learned features, baseline quality and reproducibility. Related work adds substantive ZipIt!, REPAIR and multi-teacher distillation discussion. The earlier pruning/correlation motivation and its supporting citations are removed; publication-year updates to retained works are merely bibliographic changes.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, motivation and experimental narrative. Sharded experiments precede non-IID experiments, appendix results are organized by architecture and dataset, and the broader-impact statement moves before the references. These exceed terminology or copyediting changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column presentation, with substantial table restructuring and relocation. v2 adds an algorithm-capability matrix and numerous benchmark and analysis tables, replaces the clustering display with a four-panel figure, and redraws the landscape plots with different scales and styling.

improvement.justification: v2 directly benchmarks Transformer OTFusion, which v1 could not implement, and tests broad applicability through medical/ImageNet data, compression and robustness studies. This resolves important gaps in empirical support. Clearer theoretical assumptions and attribution instructions also help. These gains outweigh reduced replication for four-way ViT fusion and lost training-epoch details. Unequal fusion budgets still limit transformer comparisons, and blanket superiority remains overstated: KD beats KF-Gradient on four- and six-way sharded CIFAR-100 in Table 17.
